title: Coalesce console hot-path requests and harden caching to cut tail latency
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Background:
The Console backend has multiple overlapping code paths that fetch and compose the same upstream entities (routes, model metadata, token-costs) for a single UI page. This leads to duplicate upstream calls, sporadic high tail latency, and noisy cache churn. Several GraphQL resolvers and REST handlers duplicate in-process LRU caching logic that diverges in key format and TTL.

Goal:
Reduce p95/p99 request latency for the Console overview and per-route pages by 30-50% under production traffic, by coalescing concurrent identical fetches, normalizing cache key schema, and consolidating cache responsibilities (in-process LRU -> single source of truth + Redis TTLs). Remove duplicated query composition layers to simplify observability and make future rollout of KV prefix caching easier.

Scope / What we'll change:
- Add a request-coalescing layer (singleflight-style) at the Console API gateway for identical upstream calls (same route+params+auth scope) to reduce duplicate remote calls during bursts.
- Unify cache key schema across GraphQL resolvers and REST handlers (prefixing by tenant and route id, consistent serialization for param maps).
- Replace two in-house LRU caches used in handlers (metrics-cache and meta-cache) with a thin local cache + Redis as authoritative secondary cache for cross-pod hits.
- Convert the largest long-polling REST handler to a chunked streaming response to reduce memory spikes and simplify backpressure semantics.
- Bump redis client from 4.2.1 -> 5.0.0 and the GraphQL framework minor version to pick up resolver-level concurrency fixes.
- Add regression tests, microbenchmarks, and a synthetic workload that reproduces the previous tail spikes.

Non-goals:
- Major API surface changes for external consumers. (No breaking schema changes.)

Risks & Mitigations:
- Risk: Coalescing could amplify errors if upstream fails for a single canonical request. Mitigation: coalescing layer will propagate a short-circuiting error path and attach request-scoped circuit-breaker counters; fallback to best-effort stale cache when upstream returns 5xx.
- Risk: Redis client upgrade could have subtle behavior changes. Mitigation: run compatibility tests, add a canary deployment for Dedicated region, keep older client available via feature flag for rollbacks.

Rollout plan:
1) Feature flag the coalescing and new cache schema per-cluster.
2) Deploy to staging and run synthetic driver for 6 hours to validate p99 improvements and failure modes.
3) Canary to 5% of production traffic in region-us-east for 24 hours with observability dashboards (latency, error-rate, cache hit/miss, coalesce-hit count).
4) Gradual ramp to 100% with automated rollback on breach of error or latency thresholds.

Observability & Metrics to add:
- coalescing.coalesced_requests_total (by route)
- coalescing.outcome{success|upstream_error|stale_cache}
- cache.normalized_keys_created_total
- cache.redis_fallback_count
- handler.streams_opened_total
- synthetic driver p50/p95/p99 comparisons (pre/post)

Notes on implementation:
- Implement singleflight coalescing in Go in console/gateway/coalesce.go with an opaque request signature computed by hashing normalized param pairs and token-scope. Keep expiry of in-flight map short (200ms default) but configurable.
- Local cache remains a tiny LRU (200 entries) used only for ultra-low-latency reads; Redis becomes primary shared cache with TTLs tuned per-key-type.
- Update GraphQL resolvers to call an adapter function (console/cache/adapter.go) so previously duplicated LRU usage is removed from resolver code.

Acceptance criteria (see acceptance_criteria field):
acceptance_criteria: Synthetic driver shows >=30% reduction in p99 for console overview under 95th percentile load compared to baseline
Coalescing layer reports >20% coalesced requests for top-10 busiest routes in canary region
No increase in 5xx error rate above 0.1% during canary; automated rollback on breach
All GraphQL and REST handlers use the normalized cache key helper (console/cache/adapter.go) and unit tests cover key serialization
Redis client upgrade has no runtime panics in staging and passes compatibility suite
End-to-end regression tests for streaming handler validate chunked payload boundaries and backpressure behavior
